provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation:
Native mechanism: make a canvas twice the input width, copy the input into the left half, and put its left-right mirror in the right half. I pushed this output through each D4 transform, worked in visible coordinates. Rotations by 90 or 270 degrees turn the side-by-side doubling into vertical stacking, and the left-right mirror becomes a top-bottom mirror (rotCW∘fliplr = flipud∘rotCW). Reflections and 180-degree rotations decide whether the unchanged input comes first or second. Because the full native output is itself left-right symmetric, the cases work out as follows:
- d4 0 and 6: input on the left, mirror on the right.
- d4 2 and 4: mirror on the left, input on the right.
- d4 1 and 7: input on top, mirror below.
- d4 3 and 5: mirror on top, input below.
The emitted program builds the doubled canvas directly along the chosen axis and stamps the input and its mirror in that order. It needs no colour roles because every pixel is copied, so the palette has no effect. It also works for rectangular grids of any size.
draft_notes.limitations: This is a pure geometric copy-and-mirror, so the demonstrations are not consulted. The constructor only produces square 3×3 grids, but the emitted code handles any H×W. When the input is already symmetric along the mirror axis, the order of input and mirror makes no difference, so there are no tie issues. I found no constructor defects or fixture contradictions: all four train pairs and the test pair match the rule.
